utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. But...

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But it was the middle of July?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: It was the view at the time that this incident confirmed the gulf between the local Muslims and the foreign Muslims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kiggell. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now give the floor to Mr. Withopf for re-examination. And then the Judges will have some questions for the witness, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Kiggell, I have a few questions for you for clarification of a number of issues that have been addressed by my learned friend -- by my learned friends on the Defence side in the course of their cross-examination. Yesterday, the issue of the reliability of the milinfosums, or more concretely, the reliability of the sources of information that was contained in milinfosums was discussed. The question is, sir, whenever an information was questionable or whenever the source of an information was questionable, was this to your knowledge made clear in the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think when we received some information, we would have some doubt about it and try and verify it by other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P100. And can the witness please also be shown Prosecution Exhibit P101.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, if I may draw your attention first to the milinfosum number 37, of 5th of June 1993, which is Prosecution Exhibit P100. On page 1 under paragraph 2 at the end, there is a section "comment." It's a five-line section. And it says: "The reliability of this information cannot be assessed." And if I may, in addition, draw your attention, sir, to the milinfosum number 55 dated 23rd of June 1993, page 3, which is paragraph 6. And under (b), the comment which reads: "The CS attempted to verify these claims by visiting the areas mentioned." And then it's further mentioned that "further investigation was impossible." Based on your experience with milinfosums, would you say that such statements on the reliability or in the event a source was questionable were always contained in milinfosums, and these two examples I just showed you were very typical examples?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's generally true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The two milinfosums can be removed from the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Kiggell, sir, your statement in the milinfosum of 31st of May in respect to the subordination of the Mujahedin was repeatedly an issue during the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination. It was the statement of the 31st of May 1993. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber and can you please repeat as to when you arrived and as to when you were assigned the liaison officer for the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned liaison officer, it must have been round about around 22nd or 23rd May, and I left that post 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is on their feet. But the question hasn't been completed. The witness is simply being asked when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but on page 46, line 4, there's an error, either in the transcript or maybe my learned friend made an error because he mentioned the milinfosum used in the examination-in-chief. Instead, it should state the milinfosum used in the cross-examination. This is in the interest of the precision of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite right. This document, P108, was produced by the Defence during the cross-examination, or rather it was used during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that's obviously completely correct. And my question did not suggest anything to the contrary. I only introduced this issue as being discussed during the examination-in-chief and during cross-examination. However, if you allow me to continue, Mr. President, with the follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Having arrived or having assigned as the liaison officer on the 22nd or 23rd of May 1993, and having made this statement contained in the milinfosum on the 31st of May 1993, would you agree that this is an early assessment?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber on what information, on what initial information this assessment was based upon.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through my discussions and meetings with various members of the Mujahedin and 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, sir, Mr. Kiggell, does this mean this statement was based on information you received from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, by his question, the Prosecutor is suggesting the answer of the witness. The witness said "on the basis of conversations with the Mujahedin and the 3rd Corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber notes that the Prosecution is indicating the fact that the witness took on his duties on the 22nd or 23rd of May. And eight days later, eight days after his arrival, he mentions in paragraph 3 of the report dated the 31st of May these matters. The Prosecution is asking him on what basis, since he had only just arrived, he mentions these facts. And the witness says that it was on the basis of the conversations he had, both within his unit and with other persons. Then the Prosecution asks him whether the other persons were members of the BiH. And he answered yes. So this is specifying the answer. Continue, Mr. Withopf. Because what was of interest was to learn, and the Defence is well aware of the context, and that is to learn the context within which this paragraph was drafted. And as you know, we attach importance to the context, as does the Prosecution. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Kiggell, sir, the statement under paragraph 8 in the milinfosum dated the 23rd of June 1993, which is Prosecution Exhibit P101, that, and I'm quoting from it, "this cell believes they are under effective control" and it's making reference to the Mujahedin. This statement is obviously different. Based on the information that you received between the 31st of May 1993 and the 23rd of June 1993, and based on information you received not only from the BiH, but also from intelligence received by BritBat based on what you got to know travelling around in the area of Zenica and having talked to a variety of individuals you detailed yesterday, did you over the time change the initial assessment you made on the 31st of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a result of seeing the intelligence reports and conversations with my colleagues, we felt that the Mujahedin were used in the offensives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were used in the offensives and also were under the effective control as it is stated in the milinfosum of the 23rd of June 1993. Is this what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir, Mr. Kiggell, to my very last line of questioning I wish to discuss with you. That's the issue of Arnauti. You have been shown a map, and you identified the location known as Arnauti. How far away is Arnauti from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be maybe about 20 kilometres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you yourself, sir, have you yourself been in Arnauti?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How long did it take you from Zenica to reach the location of Arnauti?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately half an hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what sort of vehicle did you use?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Land Rover.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kiggell, sir. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges have some questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kiggell. Just a few questions, not to take too much time again. My first questions relates to the patrol that was denied access in the neighbourhood of Fazlici. They could not pass the control post that was there. Do you remember the -- which company that was or which unit that was?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact unit. We in our British Battalion have a reconnaissance platoon. And attached to it we had reconnaissance platoons from the light dragoons regiment. So it would be in our logbook which vehicle that was and who was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you don't recall personally what officer was involved?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. My other questions are related to Arnauti. Much has been said about Arnauti. Much has been asked of you about Arnauti. I have still some supplementary questions. I heard you saying this morning that saw the Mujahedin in a camp in Arnauti. So this supposes that you had been within the camp of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was actually in the camp of Norwegians' People Aid. We met at their location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: It's not in the Mujahedin camp?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the Mujahedin camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. You spoke with -- you have been there several times, I understand, because it was a longer process of discussions between them.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I visited on a couple of occasions. I can't remember the result. In one go, we -- or we talked for the meeting -- we may have come back for two meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And this was all also in Arnauti itself.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the Norwegians' People Aid location again..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: On the other occasions did you visit the camp itself?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You've never been in the camp?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: How many representatives from the camp have you ^K met.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's about three or four people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Three or four people. High-ranking people, low-ranking people.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have any sort of rank, but they claimed to represent who ran the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The discussions about the question what were the links with the -- between the Mujahedin and the 3rd Corps, and I would pose you that question in a very specific way concerning Arnauti. The people you met there, the officers or soldiers you met who you suppose are Mujahedin, did they consider themselves to be a member of the 3rd Corps or any signs they were a member of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think it came up in the conversation. I think because they were in the 3 Corps area, I think they may had some agreement with 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: They didn't wear insignias or --

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You couldn't remember. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question that follows on the one that was just put to you. You had a discussion with these three or four Mujahedin. Did you have a discussion with them in English or were you assisted by an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assisted by an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an officer, you didn't ask them to go and visit the area. Did you ask them to accompany them to the area that they were in?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I was concentrating on resolving the issue with the Norwegian Peoples' Aid so that the aid organisation could continue in the area. And I didn't want to upset the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Mujahedin that you had a discussion with, were they armed or not?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't accurately reflect whether they were armed or not on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they had been armed, would you have informed your superiors of the fact, since there were armed men in an area that was supposed to be a sensitive, a delicate area?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not unusual to have armed people working in sort of where the aid organisations were, Zenica, perhaps. In this instance, if they were carrying arms, if wouldn't have been unusual. So therefore, there wouldn't have been a need to report it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This morning, in response to a question put to you by the Defence, you said that over a period of several days in June, you had no contact whatsoever with people from the 3rd Corps. During that period of time, what happened with your liaison officer who had been assigned to you by the 3rd Corps? He wasn't present either?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I again can't recall whether I actually got into 3 Corps and spoke to the liaison officer for those three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question: You said that you had meetings at 1800 hours, and about 20 of you attended them. You had the rank of captain in the battalion. How many other officers were there above you? How many commanders were there, and how many captains were there? Because we know that there was a Lieutenant Colonel Duncan. But between yourself and Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, were there any other officers?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported directly to Lieutenant Colonel Duncan. And he had working for him the intelligence officer. So those were our two main points of contact. Under Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, he had the majors in charge of the companies. And you'd either have other officers there who represented the logistics part of the battalion, and then also you would have other captains who were liaison officers and had the specialist roles within the British Battalion such as we had a mortar officer or an anti-tank officer would be -- normally be a captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intelligence officer, what rank did he hold?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as we know that this is the person who compiled the milinfosums, in the course of his duties, did he have other officers, NCOs or other members of the military, or did he work alone as an intelligence officer? Was there a unit that he had at his side?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a small team. And directly underneath him, he had what is called a staff sergeant. And then he had a couple of lower-ranking NCOs to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you think that my question concerns certain secret matters, don't answer it, but if you can, please do. This intelligence officer had an important role, as we can see. Did he have the financial resources to pay informers or to -- did he have technical means which would allow him to collate information? If you don't want to answer the question, don't answer it.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Defence have any other questions? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. I have a number of questions, Mr. President, as a result of the questions put to the witness by the Trial Chamber. I would like to go back to the objection raised by my colleague. The Trial Chamber commented on this on page 87, line 18.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Page 47. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would simply like to go back to this subject, Mr. President, in order to clarify something. The objection raised by the Defence at that point in time was that when responding to a question put to the witness by the Prosecution, the witness said that the information that he had on the basis of which he compiled a report came from the 3rd Corps. The witness replied that in fact the information did come from the 3rd Corps. The Defence's objection was that the information that he had at the time did not come from one source, but from two sources. I would quite simply like the witness to confirm whether the information he had at that point in time came from the 3rd Corps alone, or whether it came both from the 3rd Corps and from the meetings that he had with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, when I first arrived in the area, we assessed that the Mujahedin weren't under the control. And therefore, however, our opinion changed as time moved on. And that's where we came to the second comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Kiggell, is rather when you made that assessment, your information came from two sources. From things you had heard from 3rd Corps as well as your meetings with Mujahedin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From several people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's the only small issue I wanted to confirm. Will you agree with me, Mr. Kiggell, that -- you've mentioned that any important issue would need mention in the milinfosum. You've answered that question a number of times.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has raised with you your visit to Arnauti. And your answer to the question raised by the Trial Chamber was what you were doing at that time. And your response was your main interest was to deal with the issue of the Norwegian aid organisation to allow them to continue with their work. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in order to allow them to continue with their work, that was your focus. And their problem was the Mujahedin. ^L

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the Mujahedin, which was this problem, you never raised this problem with the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall if I had mentioned it to 3 Corps in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if you had mentioned that problem to the 3rd Corps, it would be in the milinfosum, which it is not.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been. Again, I can't accurately recall if it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A quick question concerning your liaison officer, which was also raised by the Trial Chamber. This liaison officer which was assigned to you, a gentleman called Edo --

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- to your knowledge, this gentleman, the fact that he was your liaison officer, he also had another job. To be your liaison officer was simply your point of contact.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One final question, because the Trial Chamber has discussed with you the role of your commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, with respect to intelligence. You are -- you can confirm today that Lieutenant Colonel Duncan was indeed involved in the intelligence process?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That Captain Harrison was working for him?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that Lieutenant Colonel Duncan would attend most of the briefings at 6.00 because in fact they were his orders group.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's correct. Now, do you recall Lieutenant Colonel Duncan either writing or mentioning to General Hadzihasanovic the fact that there was any doubt about the veracity of his letter that he wrote to his headquarters asking for the mudj to be expunged from the country?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him challenging this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if he had challenged this issue, it would have been something that you would have included into the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kiggell. .

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There are no further questions for the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kiggell, for having testified here. Your testimony has taken up two days. And I think it's the first time that you have testified in a court. This brought back memories of events that took place a long time ago. We would like to thank you for having answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution, by the Defence, and by the Judges. Thank you for your answers. We wish you a good trip home. And I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. And of course, we wish you all the best in your profession as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, the last witness that we have for this week, is the witness present?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, according to my information, the witness is present and available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. How long do you think your examination-in-chief will take? Because as you know, we will be working this afternoon, too. And tomorrow we will have to adjourn at 1.45. Could you tell us how long you expect the examination-in-chief to last, providing that there are no objections by the Defence, which would result in a loss of time? But how many hours do you think your examination-in-chief will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the net time, and that's excepting the issue you, Mr. President, addressed, the net time of the questioning will certainly not be longer than two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could the usher bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Can you hear me? Are you receiving the interpretation of what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. As you will be testifying in this case, you have to make a solemn declaration. Before you do so, you should inform me of your identity. Could you please tell me your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mark Bower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2nd of October 1964.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which town or village were you born in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: York.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know the town. But which country is it in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What position do you hold at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a major in the British Army, currently serving in the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what rank did you hold? What position did you have at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire, and I was a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you testify before an international court, or was this a national court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was here at the international court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the case that you testified in, and on how many occasions did you do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified for the Prosecution in the Blaskic case, and again for the Prosecution in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have already testified in two other cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have been to The Hague on two previous occasions, and this is a third occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have already testified before this Court, you are familiar with the proceedings. It is necessary for you to make the solemn declaration now. So could you please read out the text that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now. As you're already familiar with giving testimony before an international court, the information I'll provide you with will be very brief. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution. The representative of the Prosecution is to your right. He is behind the plastic lectern. After the examination-in-chief has been concluded, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will conduct their cross-examination. The three Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions at any point in time. The questions that -- will have a relation to the questions put to you by the Prosecution or by the Defence, or questions that might help determine the truth, questions that might not have been put to you by either of the parties. Before answering a question, think about your answer, because sometimes the questions are complicated. Try to answer the questions in a clear and precise manner, and if you don't understand the question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Because sometimes a number of elements can be contained within a single question. And simply saying yes or no may not be an adequate response to a question. I know that the parties do try to put precise questions to witnesses, but sometimes they forget to do so. There are two other factors that I would like to draw your attention to. The first is you have made the solemn declaration. You should not lie. If a witness gives false testimony, he could be prosecuted. And the sentence -- the penalties could be a sentence or a fine. This probably doesn't apply to you. But when one answers a question and provides information that could be used against the witness, in such cases the witness can refuse to answer the question. This is a rule that exists in Anglo-Saxon law, but the Trial Chamber could compel you to answer the question. However, if you do answer the question, you have a form of immunity because the information you provide cannot be used against you. So this is roughly speaking the manner in which your testimony will be given here. We'll continue with the hearing in the afternoon, and you will be back here tomorrow morning, too. We hope that we will conclude your testimony tomorrow morning so that you can return to the United States. Mr. Withopf, we have half an hour before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber briefly summarise your military career?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I joined the army in 1983 and was commissioned in 1985. I joined an infantry battalion and remained with that battalion throughout my career. I've served in Canada, France, Holland, Germany. I was involved in numerous tours in Northern Ireland. I was involved in the first Gulf War. Obviously the tour in Bosnia in 1993. I was involved in the operation to enter Kosovo in 1999. And I'm currently serving in the United States as an instructor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please, Major, can you please briefly elaborate on the commanding positions you had at the different points in time.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The initial part of my career for the first six years was commanding a platoon of 26 infantry soldiers. 18 months, two years of that was spent in operation in Northern Ireland. I've also commanded a company of 120 soldiers for a period of two and a half years, again, on operations in Northern Ireland, and also in Africa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that your current rank is major, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I think you already mentioned it, but can you please again inform the Trial Chamber, what was your military rank in 1993 once you were in the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I was a captain, a platoon commander of the support weapons platoon. And I was moved from that position to be a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, Major, from when to when you were deployed in the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I arrived in the Lasva valley in -- sorry, the 24th of April, and I left the 6th or 7th of November. I can't exactly remember which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Major, the dates are the dates in the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In what context did you arrive in the area of the Lasva valley?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't understand "context".

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the broader mission?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The battalion had been told to replace the Cheshire regiment, which was the 1st British Battalion which had been sent into the Lasva valley. It was to support United Nations, specifically the UNHCR, and the mandate which we had been given, the mission statement, was to provide humanitarian assistance at the request of UNHCR. But it was then later changed and Save Life was added to that mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were making reference, Major, to the area of the Lasva valley. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber where exactly you were headquartered.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The battalion headquarters was in an old school in Stara Bila, close to Vitez. But there was a company based in Gornji Vakuf. And that second company was based in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, just for clarification, Major, did your military unit form part of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, the battalion was working as part of the UNPROFOR mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Prior to arriving in Central Bosnia, did you get any briefing in respect to the situation in exactly that area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: In our base in Germany, we were given very general information as to the background and a very broad overview as to the current situation. There was very little specific information given as we were concentrating on deployment training. But on our arrival, we transited through Split, and we were given much more detailed information as we arrived. But the majority of information we received on our handover from the previous unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And Major, what was the information, the more-detailed information, about?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The detailed information we received was very much about personalities and locations, the ethnic groupings, their capabilities, their weapon systems. And also what was our part within the United Nations mission and part of our UNPROFOR mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already touched on this issue, Major, but can you please in more detail for the benefit of the Trial Chamber describe in detail what your duties have been at the time.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I was assigned as the G-5 liaison officer, which was specifically to deal with humanitarian issues. I was not required to do specific liaison with any military headquarters, either HVO or ABiH. My primary role was to forge links with the ICRC and all the NGO agencies which were currently operating in the Lasva valley. I would then also work on assessing the effectiveness of the humanitarian aid effort to act as another pair of eyes to assess the effectiveness of the UNHCR and all the NGO campaigns to try and coordinate it so that the outlying and outreaching areas who may need it but not have been visited, was to try and assess and provide input to the aid agency so they could then resolve those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber and for clarification, can you please explain what a G-5 liaison officer means.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The G-5 is a military term given to the area of humanitarian or nonmilitary assistance. So very much it's civil liaison, rather than military liaison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, in fulfilling your duties as a G-5 liaison officer, can you please describe a typical day at the time you have been in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: We could only operate in daylight hours. We found it was too risky to drive our vehicles after dark because we couldn't guarantee that the whiteness of them could be identified. So we started as soon as daylight came. I would go to Zenica, to the headquarters of the ICRC. I would brief them on the previous 24 hours' operations. I would give them any information which we had assessed which would be useful for them to ensure their safety throughout their area of operations. I would then listen any concerns they may have, any assistance they may want from me. That meeting would take approximately one hour, 90 minutes. I would then start visiting the local hospitals, starting in Zenica, working my way through Travnik, Stara Vitez, Vitez, Novi Bila. Again, very much just seeing what assistance they required were casualty evacuations required, and it -- just assessing the results of the previous 24 hours. I would make continual radio communications with the base at Stari Bila and see if I was needed elsewhere. And that would continue until daylight finished when I would then return for a briefing at 1800 hours back in the BritBat location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who at the time, Major, was your superior?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: My commanding officer was Lieutenant Colonel Alistair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to whom did Lieutenant Colonel Alistair Duncan report to? What was his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: He had a UNPROFOR chain of command to the headquarters in Kiseljak. But he also had -- there was a British national element which was in Split. But that was very much for the administration side rather than anything for the UNPROFOR mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Having provided the Trial Chamber with a comprehensive overview of a typical work day at the relevant time, in fulfilling your duties, did you travel a lot?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Every day, I would be in my vehicles travelling around. Very rarely would we spend a day sitting in the BritBat location waiting for something to happen. There was always something which needed to be doing, even if it was just going into an area which hadn't been visited for some particular time to see how the locals were feeling, what was the opinion. Were there any requirements or concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please in geographical terms describe what can be called your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It stretched from Zenica through to Travnik. It included Novi Travnik, Vitez. And it stretched into maybe 20 miles north and south of the main Travnik-Zenica road. There would be one or two occasions I would have to go further afield, Maglaj, Kakanj, but that was on specific request of aid agencies. As a general rule, I very much kept along the line of Zenica-Travnik, and 20 miles north and south of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the course of you travelling through the areas you just mentioned, to what sort of people or to what people did you talk to in order to fulfil your duties?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Initially, I would always talk to doctors or aid agencies. But as the tour progressed, I invariably needed the permission to conduct my activities from military commanders. So invariably, I would be drawn into seeking permission from the various military command, whether HVO or ABiH in the region with which I was trying to conduct a specific operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Earlier on, Major, you mentioned that your typical workday ended with an 1800 hours briefing in Vitez. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what this briefing was about and who attended it.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The 1800 hours briefing was a daily occurrence. It was chaired by Lieutenant Colonel Duncan. And it was all the primary commanders of the battalion, all the liaison officers, company commanders, operations officers. And the aim of the meeting was to inform everybody of what all units had done that day. The military information officer would give an assessment as to what he believed the action of that day, what his analysis of it was, what it may project, to try and give some idea as to where we could or couldn't go the next day, or where we should go the next day. The commanding officer would then give his opinions. He may direct specific actions to be conducted. And then he would summarise at the end of the meeting which was scheduled for about 45 minutes to an hour, on what he felt were the important issues of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: During your more than six months' stay in the area of Central Bosnia, did you always attend the 1800 hours meetings?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I attended every meeting there was except for the two weeks I was on rest and recuperation on leave back in Germany which I think was sometime in August, late August beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did others to your knowledge also, other members of BritBat obviously, did they also regularly attend the 1800 hours meetings?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was the same personalities every day. It was what we termed the command group. It was the commanders of the subunits of the formations, the people who were going to then go away and write their orders and command the soldiers in whatever operations were going to be conducted. So it was the company commanders, the liaison officers, everyone who was in -- responsible for making decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Having attended almost each and every day during your stay, during your six months' stay in the region, do you think that you could -- got a full and comprehensive picture after having attended the 1800 meetings?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The aim of those meetings was to ensure that everybody had a common view as to what was happening and what was the purpose of the next day. So certainly, I felt that I was as well-informed as anybody else as to what the situation was, who the personalities were, and what the assessments of that previous 24 hours, how we got to those assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was what has been discussed in the course of the previous meeting, was it summarised in writing?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The military information officer was produce a military information summary, which I believe is shortened to milinfosum, which was produced daily. It wasn't necessarily a record of that meeting, but it certainly held the majority of information, the salient information, which was discussed at the 1800 hours meeting. The military information summary was produced by all troops who had been on the ground in that day, would come back in and brief the military information officer as to what they had seen. They may make comment on it. And then he would collate all that information. And then much later that night, he would produce the military information summary and add comment based on his analysis of the information he had been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For what purpose, Major, was the milinfosum put together?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: There were two reasons for the military information summary. The first was it was an external document that would go up the UN chain of command, and also to our bordering units, the other international battalions, to let them know what was happening in our area as their convoys transited through our area as well. But I think the primary reason for this document was to allow what we call pattern analysis, to identify patterns in operations so that we have a reference document to go back to to try and identify trends, to try and predict what is going to happen so we can offer the best advice to the agencies with which we are charged with dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The milinfosums, as you describe them, being a pattern analysis, can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the reliability of the information contained in the milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The information is what whoever had been on the ground, liaison officers, patrols, had seen with their eyes or they had learned with the use of interpreters when speaking to locals or wherever they had been. They would then come back and give that information over. So it was very much a one-to-one opinion view or something that had been seen on the ground. So it was a collation of all this raw data. And it was difficult to confirm all the time from a second, third, or fourth source, as we didn't have -- and there was no requirement to have human intelligence or any electronic intelligence-gathering means. That's not why we were there. So it was a very much what had been seen that day. That was why it was called military information and not military intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Moving on to a different subject, Major, earlier on you were informing the Trial Chamber that you were travelling a lot within the area you have detailed. Were you allowed to travel freely in this area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The majority of time, I was allowed to travel pretty much where I wanted to go, but there were times when my travelling down main routes or side roads was blocked when I came to checkpoints. These checkpoints, majority of the times, were the front lines between two opposing forces. But occasionally, the checkpoints would appear behind the front lines and would invariably require us to go up the respective HVO or ABiH military chain of command to get authority to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Which was the competent ABiH chain of command to get such permissions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Invariably, I was sent to the 3 Corps headquarters to get permission to travel through the checkpoints which I needed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who was responsible for providing such permissions? With whom did you deal in asking such permissions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The majority of the time, I would deal with a Colonel Merdan. But I believe once when Colonel Merdan wasn't available, I saw General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was General Hadzihasanovic's position at the time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I understand that the general was the commander of 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was Colonel Merdan's position at the time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I made the conclusion that Colonel Merdan was a military assistant, or he coordinated his outer office. Somebody who worked closely with the general who could give permission on the general's authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you ever been in General Hadzihasanovic's office, 3rd Corps headquarters office?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I recall a time when Colonel Merdan wasn't there. I went into an office. I believe it was the general's, because the general was there, but I can't honestly say if it was his specific office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This office in which you met Mr. Hadzihasanovic, how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I would say it would be a typical three-star general's office. Good furniture. There wasn't the trappings or paraphernalia of an operations room. So, no banks of radios, no plethora of map boards with traces written all over them. It was what I would call a smart office. Chairs to sit down in for the guests, or visitors. There was a map on the wall from what I can recall. But it wasn't an operations room, per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In saying it was a typical three-star general's office, was it similar to the ones you experienced within NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: When I was involved with headquarters ARK, I worked for a three-star general. It was very similar. An outer office, followed by the general's office, which I would equate to a large businessman's office, rather than what people may expect as a military office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Coming back to the issue of granting approval to go through checkpoints, were such permissions always given when you asked for them?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Generally, the permission could be achieved, not necessarily immediately. Sometimes there would be some delay or some bargaining, some negotiations. But occasionally, permission was refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your recollection and to your knowledge, did you get to know why occasionally permission was refused?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: We were never specifically told why permission was refused to cross checkpoints or to have access to areas. We could make educated assessments due to information which other units, other patrols had seen. We came to the conclusion that it was inconvenient for UNPROFOR to be in that area because something was happening which necessarily the forces didn't want us to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The forces didn't want you to see, does this include the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the assessment I had to make for denial of access to one of the routes which I regularly used for evacuating wounded or dying civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Having been in the area of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH 3rd Corps from April to November 1993, how would you describe the relationship between BritBat and ABiH 3rd Corps over the time?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The impression which I got from the commanding officer was that the relationship was actually very good, and that generally there was a willingness to try and work through any difficulties. But generally, I would say it was a good relationship. I can't speak for Colonel Duncan, but the impression he gave me was that he had no specific problems when he went to 3 Corps. It was not something that he did not look forward to. He found it quite a -- sort of a professional relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Over the time from April to November 1993, did you yourself experience a change of the habits and of the relationship between you and ABiH 3rd Corps officers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I would say that the relationship changed around mid or late September in 1993. Up until that time, in the area which I was working in, the HVO appeared to be in the ascendancy and were causing the majority of the casualties on the Bosnian Muslim side. So I was very much involved in dealing with the Bosnian Muslim casualties. But in September, there seemed to be a specific shift in the fortunes of the two warring sides. And the HVO began receiving and, if anything, lost the initiative. And it was at that time that we were trying to shift our emphasis dealing with Bosnian Croat casualties. And I found that I couldn't always get the assistance that I needed at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Could you please, Major, expand a bit on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: One of the hospitals which I visited on a regular basis was the makeshift hospital in Novi Bila set up in a monastery. And as a result of the changing fortunes of the fighting at that time in September, there was a large increase in the number of casualties at that hospital to the stage that it was overflowing. They didn't have the resources, the doctors or the medical supplies with which to deal with, not just the resultants of war, the battle trauma, but the day-to-day injuries: People still got cancer, people still had broken limbs or the general illnesses. So there were significant requests for evacuation of casualties to the number of 50 or 60 at the time, rather than the two or three which I was used to dealing with. And to move 50 or 60 seriously wounded people, the plan was to move them to Kiseljak, and then from Kiseljak they would be moved to Split. That required the cooperation of all sides, because we would have to travel down a road which was the front line between the BiH and HVO forces, between the Cajdras feature and Vitez. So it took considerable negotiation on behalf of the military liaison officers and myself to ensure we had a window of opportunity with which to move these people. It was a fairly large undertaking. There were times when it was denied or permission was initially given. And I remember one specific instance, we'd actually loaded the casualties onto the backs of trucks, and then the permission was denied by 3rd Corps. So we had to unload the casualties and take them back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Major, which military units of the ABiH 3rd Corps did operate within the area which can be described as your area of responsibility as you detailed earlier on today?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I specifically remember the 325 mountain brigade, because that was the primary route that I would use to travel to Zenica on the mountain road which went by the Cajdras checkpoint. And that was the main unit which I really had difficulties dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, which ABiH 3rd Corps unit operated in the area of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I don't recall the unit, the unit name which operated in Zenica itself. But I know that next to the ICRC headquarters, just up from the ICRC headquarters, heading towards the mountain road, the back road heading through the Cajdras checkpoint, at the music school there was the headquarters of the 7 Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I think it would be advisable to have the break now, since I wish to enter into a different sort of questioning later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're going to have a break. And we will resume work at 5 to 1.00. Then we will continue until 1.45. Then have an hour break, and resume at 2.45. So we will resume at 5 to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, we have 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, prior to the break, you informed the Trial Chamber that in the music school in Zenica, there was the 7th Muslim Brigade. During your time in Central Bosnia between April and November 1993, what did you get to know about the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The information which was given to us, and whether it's from military briefings, contained in the military information summary, but also what I saw travelling through Zenica and seeing the headquarters, was that it was a military unit within 3 Corps. It was part of their operational units which could be deployed as part of their plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: From what you got to know, Major, was the 7th Muslim Brigade of any particular significance for the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was assessed by the British Battalion that we would sort of term the 7th Muslim Brigade as a combat indicator. And by that I mean, where a main effort was being planned or where a specific action was required that was essential, then 7 Muslim Brigade would be in that area rather than in a supporting effort. It was very much a, I would say a primary unit, not necessarily used as a terrain-holding unit for manning checkpoints, and remaining in a static position for a long time. It appeared to be a unit which was part of the manoeuvre element employed by the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you, please, Major explain on the phrase "combat" -- expand on the phrase "combat indicator." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The phrase combat indicator is a term which the military use as part of our information assessment. We try and create through this pattern analysis I talked about earlier of logging incidents which on their own may seem insignificant, but when viewed with hindsight, retrospectively, it can create a pattern, a pattern leading to a subsequent action. And so if we can identify these patterns, we will then, if we see these patterns forming again, be able to predict as to what future operations may be happening. And we identified that 7 Muslim Brigade was one such combat indicator, that they were an important unit because they were always involved where the main fighting was taking place. So if we could track the location of a combat indicator unit, and in this case, 7 Muslim Brigade, we hoped to identify where the next battles were going to take place. Because ultimately, the aftermath of those battles is where the aid is going to be required or where I was going to have to try and bring in more medical aid or evacuate casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: On what you've seen and from what you got to know having attended regularly the 1800 hours meetings and having talked to the variety of people you mentioned earlier on, were there foreign fighters within the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was known that even before we arrived in Central Bosnia that there were mercenaries. And that was the phrase that was initially used, that there were mercenaries in Central Bosnia, because we were advised what to do when British mercenaries approached us for assistance. But it became they clear early in the tour that there were -- there was an element of 7 Muslim Brigade who were more -- although they were adhering to stricter Islamic codes, and they were termed the Mujahedin element of 7 Muslim Brigade. And I came across them in large numbers once early in May, early in the tour. And it was quite apparent that they were from either the Middle East. There was one from Great Britain. At least one from Great Britain, which we identified. And there was -- there were a couple that I saw from North Africa. The best estimate which we can guess of where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, from what you got to know and from what you've seen yourself, and from what you got to know from having talking to the variety of people you mentioned earlier on, in the early stages of your tour in Central Bosnia where these foreigners which were referred to as Mujahedin, were they part of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The assessment which I came to, and it was generally felt that they were part of 7 Muslim Brigade. They certainly operated as a formed unit. The foreign element which we termed "Mujahedin" didn't operate in 1's and 2's or small numbers spread throughout the 7 Muslim Brigade. They were a formed unit. They certainly kept together and were concentrated, rather than spread across the whole fighting element within the area which we were operating in the Lasva valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were mentioning, Major, that the Mujahedin could be identified as people from Arab countries. Why could they be identified as people from Arab countries?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I was able to identify them, having served in Kuwait, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia. But generally by their features. There were a number who I would say may even have come from the Afghan -- Afghanistan-style, by their style of dress, how they wore their facial hair, their beards. And their attitudes towards us. It was markedly different from the regular ABiH who we had day-to-day dealings with. They were -- at times, very intimidating, and they were people to be very wary of. Because I got the impression that they were generally unpredictable in how they may react to general requests. For example, some of them would refuse to use our female interpreters. They only wanted to speak to us through male interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please, Major, can you please inform the Trial Chamber about what you have seen in respect to the weaponry of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I saw the Mujahedin were equipped with the standard Kalashnikov AK47s, but they also had RPG 7 rocket launchers. The majority of them carried large knives, not the small knife I would considered called a bayonet. Much larger knives, hunting knives, which were brandishing just as a matter of emphasis more than anything else. They appeared to be well equipped for fighting, and they had this confidence in themselves, and bordering on arrogance. And it was a difficult element to deal with when we came across them, because we generally came across them by accident rather than by any planning because they moved. They were a manoeuvre element. We couldn't predict where they were going to be. We had to try and track them, and that meant finding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform, Major, the Trial Chamber about the uniforms, if any, the Mujahedin wore at the time.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The time when I came across the Mujahedin was in May, and the weather was not particularly good. So the majority of them had some semblance of a camouflage uniform on. Invariably, they didn't have matching camouflage jackets and camouflage trousers. It would be one or the other. But what I did notice was that they would -- the majority of them had the Shemagues wrapped around their heads hiding their faces. There were a number which would have, I would call, a traditional Taliban-style hat, soft-felt hat on the tops of their heads with exposings of a very full beard. The majority, I would say, didn't have camouflage trousers on, but they had camouflage jackets. Some had badges either on the pockets of their uniform, on the sleeves. And they appeared to be well equipped. They certainly didn't seem to lack the ability to resupply themselves or move around the areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, you were informing us that at the early stages of your tour in Central Bosnia, and you started your tour in April 1993, you saw the Mujahedin or you got to know that the Mujahedin you just described were together with the 7th Muslim Brigade. How are the Mujahedin within the 7th Muslim Brigade, how are they linked to the phrase you used earlier on today, namely, "combat indicator"?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Because we identified through either Mujahedin prisoners or Mujahedin dead, which had been informed to us by HVO because they wanted to use them in exchange, we could certainly track where they had been involved in the fighting. And they always appeared where the fighting was the heaviest. So to us, it appeared that the 7 Muslim Brigade and Mujahedin were a mobile, main effort force that was used to, whether it be to spearhead or reinforce the main effort attack or the main effort assault. And as I said, not be wasted on manning checkpoints in a static environment. And so that's what was the key thing for us. I equated them to my dealings with the Djukara [phoen] in the HVO in that aspect of they were a unit which had to be tracked because wherever they were, then something was liable to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Something was liable to happen. What does it mean, in more concrete terms, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: We mean that ultimately, if they are near the front lines, that is where the main effort attack is going to be weighted. It's probably where the majority of the assets have been moved to, to assist in that attack. And we know that that's ultimately where the humanitarian effort, which I was going to be involved in, would be heaviest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Something was likely or was liable to happen, does it make reference to attacks by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. An operation of an offensive nature which could be an attack or an assault, either seizing terrain or destroying enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just a few minutes ago, Major, you mentioned the Mujahedin spearheading attacks. Can you please in some more detail, inform the Trial Chamber what you mean by the Mujahedin spearheading attacks, ABiH attacks?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: What I mean is that where the Mujahedin 7 Muslim Brigade were, it is certainly where the fighting would be the most intense, and we could expect that that would be the prolonged main effort for the attack, that it is something which was, as I say, this combat indicator. It was of great importance that that's where this unit would be. It was -- it happened on a number of occasions, and it was too many occasions for it to be circumstance or coincidence, that wherever the main effort was, as part of the overall campaign within the six months we were there and witnessed the overall campaign, for it to be coincidence. It was too coordinated for this unit to just be in the right place at the right time on a battlefield, more than once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This unit, and I'm asking you, Major, whether you're making reference to this unit, is this, just for clarification, the 7th Muslim Brigade with the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. "This unit," I'm referring to the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Earlier on, Major, you were mentioning that you were yourself being involved in the exchange of Mujahedin soldiers. How were such exchanges organised? Was the ABiH command involved in it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The initial request would either come through military liaison that HVO had a number of dead or captured ABiH and would want an exchange for their respective dead or captured from that engagement. I would then arrange with the ICRC, who would lead in any prisoner release, prisoner negotiation. But ultimately, anything like that required again cease-fires of both sides, because invariably it would be done within the front lines, the no-man's-land between the battle lines. And invariably, it was done with the ICRC leading, but they required us to create the conditions to set the continues to allow the prison exchange and also the dead-body verification. The majority of the times, they wouldn't just accept us bringing dead bodies across the front line. We had to collect the bodies, lay them out for independent ABiH and HVO to verify that the dead bodies were who they claimed to be. And if they weren't, then the exchange would be cancelled, and we would have to try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this mean, Major, just for clarification, that the ABiH 3rd Corps command was involved in organising and facilitating such exchanges of Mujahedin soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly we used the ABiH chain of command. At times, we would be informed by ABiH that they wanted certain Mujahedin back, either prisoner or their dead. And there would have to be some quid pro quo release of somebody from their side, an HVO dead, HVO prisoners would have to be released. And the authority for the release of these people, although the HVO may well have been detained at a much lower level at the front line, there was quite clearly no ability to make a decision at that lowest level to release HVO prisoners or HVO bodies. We always ended up having to go back up the chain of command. And this was a continual process and a continual repeat performance. Everything ultimately we came back for -- big issues, back to 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, do you know Mr. Vaughan Kent-Payne?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I know Vaughan Kent-Payne. He was an officer in our battalion. He was the company commander of Charlie Company during the six-month tour in 1993 in Bosnia. And I knew him before we deployed to Bosnia. And I'm still friends with him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recall a situation, Major, in which you and Vaughan Kent-Payne travelled into the area -- into the wider area of Bandol and Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I remember the incident in May. I can't remember the exact time. I know it was early in the tour, because the weather hadn't really turned into the full heat of summer. But I had received a request from Thomas Osario, who worked for the United Nations High Commission for refugees. I believe he was an investigator of some sort. And he approached me on a Friday or a Saturday with a badly drawn sketch map which he said had been given to him by a refugee who had witnessed the killing of civilians. And he said this map indicated where there was a mass grave. He -- Thomas Osario asked me, as the humanitarian officer, if I could go into the area around Guca Gora, Bandol, Maljine, to see if I could find this mass grave. The difficulty was this was after a main ABiH assault on Guca Gora, so it was still quite a tense area. So I couldn't travel in my own softskin vehicles. I needed armoured protection to go in there. So I used Vaughan Kent-Payne's vehicles. He used his two Warrior armoured fighting vehicles to take myself, interpreter, and Randy Rhodes, who was the UN representative to the battalion. We left on a Sunday to go. I know it was a Sunday because it is unusual for us to be using armoured vehicles on a Sunday. It was normally a maintenance day, to prepare all our equipment for the remaining days. And I travelled in the back of Vaughan Kent-Payne's vehicle with Randy Rhodes and the interpreter. And we stopped at Guca Gora. We stopped at Guca Gora because our route was blocked by the Mujahedin, who were -- there were a dozen of them congregated around the church in Guca Gora. And we had the mortar hatches open in the back of the vehicle. So as I was looking out, my head would have been the height of the grass around the church because the road is sunken by the side of the church. The Mujahedin, some of them were coming out of the church. There was a lot of furniture outside the church. And they were quite agitated by us, by our presence. They were well armed. There was an RPG 7 rocket launcher. They had a heavy machine-gun. The majority of them were armed with AK47s. Initially, they wouldn't engage us in discussion because they refused to talk to us through our female interpreter, which caused some significant problems to try and negotiate either our withdrawal or our continued mission. We noticed that there was an English accent among them, specifically from west Yorkshire which is where my battalion recruit's from. He wouldn't engage us in conversation either. And one of the Mujahedin negligently discharged his rifle. So he mistakenly fired his rifle. Fortunately it didn't come in our direction. It went over our heads. I don't know which one it was that -- that opened fire. That caused a bit of a standoff. We traversed our turrets, and we all made ready and waited for something else to happen. Fortunately, it didn't. There was a very long pause. And I think that forced negotiation, face had been lost, I think, on the part of the Mujahedin, so they entered into negotiations with us. But they refused to let the vehicles progress towards Maljine. Vaughan Kent-Payne managed to persuade the Mujahedin to take us in a vehicle. And by us, I mean myself, Randy Rhodes, and Vaughan, but we had to leave our weapons behind. So we left our rifles. We didn't have any radios. We just had this sketch map. And when I look back on it, I would suggest it was military naivete on our part to actually put ourselves in their hands. We'd been in -- in the theatre maybe six or seven weeks and it was my first encounter with the Mujahedin and I think it may have been Vaughan Kent-Payne's. We were driven along a road to a village, and I don't know which village we were taken to. I was in the back of a pickup truck. And all I had was a sketch map. The sketch map had no reference points on it, no north pointers. It was just a road, a barn, high ground, and X marks the spot, as it were. As we were travelling down the road, we continually saw Mujahedin walking in both directions. They were greeting each other with the traditional "Allah-HU-Akbar." And it was quite apparent we were in the middle of the Mujahedin. We stopped at a village which some of the houses were still habitable, but were being searched. The animals had all been killed. And we were allowed to walk around with our guides, for wont of a better phrase, but were unable to correspond the sketch map to the ground we were at. What we could see was across the valley, a village was on fire. So we decided we were going to achieve nothing where we were. I think Vaughan had given a cutoff time of one hour to his remaining vehicles, that if we had not returned they were to come and find us. But how they were going to do that, I'm not quite sure. We returned to the vehicles, and we negotiated our way back out of Guca Gora, and made our way to the smoking village which we then found to be Bandol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Having been in Guca Gora, Major, what actually have you seen in Guca Gora whilst there?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I didn't see the -- our route into Guca Gora because I was in the back of the vehicle. I actually came out of the vehicle when we stopped, so that was at the church. So I didn't see the whole village. But what I could see, some of the -- some of the houses were clearly were being ransacked in the fact that their furniture was outside. I didn't see people physically throwing anything out, so how it happened, whether it was during the fighting or whatever, I can't comment. But certainly it was clear that there had been a lot of movement through that -- through the area which I could see. And specifically, the church, because during the evacuation of the Croat population from the church, it certainly wasn't in the state which we then found it in. A lot of the furniture was outside the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Just a technical comment I would like to make. I'm referring to the question put to my learned colleague from the Prosecution. The witness said that this was the first time he had contact with the Mujahedin, and this part of the witness's answer hasn't been recorded in the transcript. Perhaps this is something that the witness could confirm or clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this incident was the first time which I had certainly come across the Mujahedin. And I believe it was the first time that Major Vaughan Kent-Payne had come across the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At that day, and I'm referring to the day you saw the Mujahedin in the area of Guca Gora, once you left the area, did you also come across soldiers of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was difficult to try and differentiate between the two, other than their appearance. We certainly left Guca Gora to extract ourselves from the area, once we had tried to find the site. And we then transited through, if I could phrase it, as regular ABiH people from that region, rather than foreigners, foreign mercenaries. So there was -- it was like a buffer period before we then got to the front line and then came back towards our BritBat location. Whether they were 7 Muslim Brigade or a regular ABiH unit I couldn't honestly say. But there was a definite -- an area where we found the Mujahedin, then there were ABiH soldiers from the region of Yugoslavia and former Yugoslavia, and then we crossed into HVO territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
